title: Antony goes into the desert
hook: a young Egyptian hears 'go and sell that thou hast' read in church, and does it, and in time walks into the desert

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cyprian, and two cities where Christians nursed the sick through a plague. Your line: they stayed.

A young man in an Egyptian village has just buried his parents. He's inherited good farmland, and he's responsible for his little sister. Walking to church, he's turning something over: the apostles left everything to follow Jesus, and in the book of Acts, believers sold their land and laid the money at the apostles' feet. What would that look like now? He walks in, and at that moment the Gospel being read is the one about a rich young man. His name is Antony. His Life was written by Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria.

Here's the verse he heard, from Matthew, in the King James Bible: "If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come and follow me." Athanasius says Antony felt the words had been read for him. In the Gospel, the rich young man goes away sorrowful. Antony goes out and does it. He gives his family's land to the people of his village, sells the rest, and gives the money to the poor, keeping a little back for his sister. Then he walks into church again and hears another line: "Take therefore no thought for the morrow." So he gives away what he'd kept, places his sister with a community of faithful women, and begins a life of prayer and work. He doesn't vanish into the sand that afternoon. He starts at the edge of his village, learning from an old man who lives that way, moves out to the tombs, and only later crosses into the desert, farther and farther in. Athanasius says he wrote the Life because monks in other places asked what Antony was like. Catholic and Orthodox churches honor Antony as a father of monastic life, and there the call to sell everything is a real vocation some are given. Other Christians, among them some Protestants, read the verse as aimed at what holds a person's heart, and practice it through generosity rather than leaving home. Both readings take the verse seriously. What lands is the speed. He heard. And he went.
screen: `THE VILLAGE EDGE, THE TOMBS, THE DESERT.`
`A VOCATION, OR A MATTER OF THE HEART?`

segments.voice: Walk in your mind through a closet, a shelf or a drawer, and find one thing you don't need that someone else could use, not the easiest junk but something with a little weight to it. Decide where it would go; if you pray, offer it to God as you let it go, and if not, hold it in your mind and open your hand.
Antony. A young Egyptian who heard go and sell that thou hast, gave it away, and step by step walked into a life of prayer in the desert.
Your line: he heard, and went. No waiting to feel ready. Day seven hundred sixty-five, done.

howItsDone: Catholic and Orthodox churches honor Antony as a father of monasticism and keep his feast; monks and nuns take vows of poverty, while other Christians practice the same verse through giving and simple living.

chat.says: Did Antony walk straight into the desert the day he heard that verse?
options: No, step by step: first the edge of his village, then the tombs, then the desert.
Yes, that same afternoon, leaving his little sister for the village to raise.
No, he kept his land for years and only left once his sister was married.
chat.meaning: Athanasius tells it in stages: Antony learned from an old man at the village edge, moved out to the tombs, and only later went into the desert.

Athanasius.meaning: the bishop of Alexandria who wrote the Life of Antony

monastic.meaning: to do with monks and nuns and their life of prayer

notes: The index dates this 'c. 270'; the script states no date and no age (Life 1–2 gives his age at his parents' death). Confirm.
The index says he 'walks into the desert'; the script follows the Life's stages (village edge and an old ascetic, 3; the tombs, 8; the desert mountain, 11–12). Confirm chapter numbers.
Land given to villagers (Life 2 gives a number of arourae; the script omits it); sister placed with 'known and faithful virgins' (3). Paraphrased.
Church differences: Catholic and Orthodox honor Antony as a father of monasticism; 'other Christians, among them Protestant churches' read Matthew 19:21 as about the heart. Confirm fairness.
Original: μοναχός from μόνος (standard lexicon etymology). It is not a word from the day's sources; Keeper may prefer null.
